claim: Exocytosis is an active vesicle trafficking process by which eukaryotes secrete materials to the extracellular environment and insert membrane proteins into the plasma membrane.
source: Exocytosis is an active vesicle trafficking process by which eukaryotes secrete materials to the extracellular environment and insert membrane proteins into the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about exocytosis that represents established scientific knowledge in the field of cell biology.

claim: The final step of exocytosis in yeast involves the assembly of two t-SNAREs, Sso1/2 and Sec9, with the v-SNARE, Snc1/2, on secretory vesicles.
source: The final step of exocytosis in yeast involves the assembly of two t-SNAREs, Sso1/2 and Sec9, with the v-SNARE, Snc1/2, on secretory vesicles.
evidence: This statement describes the molecular mechanism of exocytosis in yeast, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: The rate-limiting step in exocytosis is the formation of a binary complex of the two t-SNAREs.
source: The rate-limiting step in this process is the formation of a binary complex of the two t-SNAREs.
evidence: This statement identifies a specific mechanistic bottleneck in the exocytosis process, representing established knowledge about SNARE assembly kinetics.

claim: Sec3 accelerates binary complex assembly.
source: Despite a previous report of acceleration of binary complex assembly by Sec3, it remains unknown how Sso2 is efficiently recruited to the vesicle-docking site marked by Sec3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work, as indicated by the phrase 'previous report'.

claim: The crystal structure of the pleckstrin homology (PH) domain of Sec3 in complex with a nearly full-length version of Sso2 lacking only its C-terminal transmembrane helix was determined.
source: Here, we report a crystal structure of the pleckstrin homology (PH) domain of Sec3 in complex with a nearly full-length version of Sso2 lacking only its C-terminal transmembrane helix.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including crystallography and structure determination.

claim: The structure shows a previously uncharacterized binding site for Sec3 at the N-terminus of Sso2, consisting of two highly conserved triple residue motifs (NPY: Asn-Pro-Tyr).
source: The structure shows a previously uncharacterized binding site for Sec3 at the N-terminus of Sso2, consisting of two highly conserved triple residue motifs (NPY: Asn-Pro-Tyr).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The two NPY motifs bind Sec3 synergistically.
source: We further reveal that the two NPY motifs bind Sec3 synergistically, which together with the previously reported binding interface constitute dual-site interactions between Sso2 and Sec3 to drive the fusion of secretory vesicles at target sites on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC experiments showing that the two motifs together bind more strongly than either motif alone.

claim: The dual-site interactions between Sso2 and Sec3 drive the fusion of secretory vesicles at target sites on the plasma membrane.
source: We further reveal that the two NPY motifs bind Sec3 synergistically, which together with the previously reported binding interface constitute dual-site interactions between Sso2 and Sec3 to drive the fusion of secretory vesicles at target sites on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the structural and functional data presented in the study.

claim: Inter-organelle material exchange is carried out primarily through membrane traffic in which membrane bound transport vesicles bud from a donor compartment and are delivered to a specific acceptor compartment.
source: Inter-organelle material exchange is carried out primarily through membrane traffic in which membrane bound transport vesicles bud from a donor compartment and are delivered to a specific acceptor compartment.
evidence: This is a general statement about cellular trafficking mechanisms representing established knowledge.

claim: Upon arriving at the destination, cargo-packed vesicles are first recognized and caught by tethering factors situated on the target membrane, which then hand the captured vesicles over to the SNARE proteins that drive membrane fusion.
source: Upon arriving at the destination, cargo-packed vesicles are first recognized and caught by tethering factors situated on the target membrane, which then hand the captured vesicles over to the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor-attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins that drive membrane fusion (Ungermann and Kümmel, 2019; Chia and Gleeson, 2014; Bröcker et al., 2010; Yu and Hughson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work in the field.

claim: In neuronal exocytosis, fusion of synaptic vesicles to the presynaptic plasma membrane is driven by the assembly of a four-helix bundle containing two t-SNAREs, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25, on the target membrane and the v-SNARE, synaptobrevin, on synaptic vesicles.
source: In neuronal exocytosis, fusion of synaptic vesicles to the presynaptic plasma membrane is driven by the assembly of a four-helix bundle containing two t-SNAREs, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25, on the target membrane and the v-SNARE, synaptobrevin, on synaptic vesicles (Fernandez et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: SNARE assembly is tightly regulated by multiple auxiliary proteins, including the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) family of proteins, tethering factors, and small GTPases.
source: Extensive studies have established that SNARE assembly is tightly regulated by multiple auxiliary proteins, including the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) family of proteins, tethering factors, and small GTPases (Dulubova et al., 1999; Fiebig et al., 1999; Demircioglu et al., 2014; Takemoto et al., 2018; Koike and Jahn, 2019; Cai et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Munc18 is a chaperone protein that maintains syntaxin-1 in an activated conformation and passes it to its cognate SNARE partners for assembly to catalyze membrane fusion.
source: Munc18 is a chaperone protein that maintains syntaxin-1 in an activated conformation and passes it to its cognate SNARE partners for assembly to catalyze membrane fusion (Wang et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2018; Jiao et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2010; André et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on Munc18 function.

claim: The exocytic vesicle-docking site in yeast is marked by the octameric exocyst complex, which belongs to the CATCHR family of multi-subunit tethering proteins.
source: The exocytic vesicle-docking site in yeast is marked by the octameric exocyst complex, which belongs to the CATCHR family of multi-subunit tethering proteins (Pleskot et al., 2015; Guo et al., 1999; Boehm and Field, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work characterizing the exocyst complex.

claim: The main function of the exocyst is to capture secretory vesicles at sites of cell surface growth, which include the tip of the daughter cell early in the cell cycle, and the mother-daughter cell junction late in the cycle.
source: The main function of the exocyst is to capture secretory vesicles at sites of cell surface growth, which include the tip of the daughter cell early in the cell cycle, and the mother-daughter cell junction late in the cycle (Lipschutz and Mostov, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on exocyst function.

claim: The two t-SNAREs for exocytosis in yeast are Sso1/2 and Sec9, which are homologs of syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25, respectively.
source: The two t-SNAREs for exocytosis in yeast are Sso1/2 and Sec9, which are homologs of syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast SNARE proteins and their homology to mammalian counterparts.

claim: The v-SNARE attached to secretory vesicles in yeast is Snc1/2, which is equivalent to synaptobrevin in neuronal exocytosis.
source: The v-SNARE attached to secretory vesicles in yeast is Snc1/2, which is equivalent to synaptobrevin in neuronal exocytosis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast v-SNARE proteins and their homology to mammalian counterparts.

claim: One of the exocyst components, Sec3, promotes SNARE assembly by interacting with the t-SNARE Sso2.
source: Our previous work showed that one of the exocyst components, Sec3, promotes SNARE assembly by interacting with the t-SNARE Sso2 (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Sec3 consists of an N-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain, a central putative coiled coil, and a C-terminal helical domain.
source: Sec3 consists of an N-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain, a central putative coiled coil, and a C-terminal helical domain.
evidence: This is a structural description of Sec3 based on established knowledge.

claim: Sso2 consists of four helices, with the first three (Habc) forming an inhibitory domain and the last (H3) serving as the SNARE motif that interacts with the other two SNAREs during membrane fusion.
source: Like syntaxin-1 and other related t-SNAREs, Sso2 consists of four helices, with the first three (Habc) forming an inhibitory domain and the last (H3) serving as the SNARE motif that interacts with the other two SNAREs during membrane fusion.
evidence: This is a structural description of Sso2 based on established knowledge about syntaxin-like proteins.

claim: The Sec3 PH domain binds to the auto-inhibited four-helix bundle of Sso2 and promotes a conformational change of the linker between Hc and H3 of Sso2 via an allosteric effect.
source: We have shown that the Sec3 PH domain binds to the auto-inhibited four-helix bundle of Sso2 and promotes a conformational change of the linker between Hc and H3 of Sso2 via an allosteric effect (Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The conformational change promoted by Sec3 binding promotes the release of the SNARE motif (H3) of Sso2 and substantially accelerates the formation of the initial binary complex between H3 of Sso2 and the two helices of the other t-SNARE, Sec9.
source: This change promotes the release of the SNARE motif (H3) of Sso2 and substantially accelerates the formation of the initial binary complex between H3 of Sso2 and the two helices of the other t-SNARE, Sec9.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the authors' previous work.

claim: A stable binary complex of Sso2 (aa1-270) and Sec3 PH domain (aa75-260) was obtained via size exclusion chromatography.
source: A stable binary complex was obtained via size exclusion chromatography (SEC) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which was then crystallized by hanging drop vapor diffusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by the SEC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diffraction data to 2.19 Å resolution was collected at the ESRF synchrotron site.
source: Diffraction data to 2.19 Å resolution was collected at the ESRF synchrotron site and the crystal structure was determined by the molecular replacement method.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental data collection.

claim: The crystal structure was determined by the molecular replacement method.
source: Diffraction data to 2.19 Å resolution was collected at the ESRF synchrotron site and the crystal structure was determined by the molecular replacement method.
evidence: This is a statement about the method used for structure determination.

claim: The crystal belongs to space group P1 (a=50.96 Å, b=58.40 Å, c=83.29 Å; α=104.28°, β=98.49°, γ=113.20°).
source: The crystal belongs to space group P1 (a=50.96 Å, b=58.40 Å, c=83.29 Å; α=104.28°, β=98.49°, γ=113.20°).
evidence: This is crystallographic data from the structure determination.

claim: The final structure was refined to Rwork and Rfree of 19.9% and 23.9%, respectively, with an average B factor of 40.74 Å2 for all macromolecules.
source: The final structure was refined to Rwork and Rfree of 19.9% and 23.9%, respectively, with an average B factor of 40.74 Å2 for all macromolecules (Table 1).
evidence: This is crystallographic refinement data presented in Table 1.

claim: The final model contains two copies of the Sso2/Sec3 complex per asymmetric unit, together with 418 ordered water molecules.
source: The final model contains two copies of the Sso2/Sec3 complex per asymmetric unit, together with 418 ordered water molecules.
evidence: This is a description of the contents of the crystal structure.

claim: One of the complexes contains residues 4–8, 33–149, and 197–226 of Sso2 and residues 76–250 of Sec3.
source: One of the complexes contains residues 4–8, 33–149, and 197–226 of Sso2 and residues 76–250 of Sec3; the other contains residues 6–14, 33–148, and 196–226 of Sso2 and residues 76–250 of Sec3.
evidence: This is a description of the visible residues in the crystal structure.

claim: The other complex contains residues 6–14, 33–148, and 196–226 of Sso2 and residues 76–250 of Sec3.
source: One of the complexes contains residues 4–8, 33–149, and 197–226 of Sso2 and residues 76–250 of Sec3; the other contains residues 6–14, 33–148, and 196–226 of Sso2 and residues 76–250 of Sec3.
evidence: This is a description of the visible residues in the crystal structure.

claim: Corresponding regions in the two complex structures are essentially identical, with r.m.s.d. of 0.45 Å for all aligned backbone atoms.
source: Corresponding regions in the two complex structures are essentially identical, with r.m.s.d. of 0.45 Å for all aligned backbone atoms (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the two structures in the asymmetric unit.

claim: Primary sequence alignments of Sso2 homologs from various yeast species reveal two conserved three-residue motifs toward the N-terminus of Sso2.
source: Primary sequence alignments of Sso2 homologs from various yeast species reveal two conserved three-residue motifs toward the N-terminus of Sso2, which we name as NPY motifs.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The double NPY motifs are connected to the highly conserved core of Sso2 (i.e. Habc and H3) via a non-conserved linker with variable lengths in different homologs.
source: These double NPY motifs are connected to the highly conserved core of Sso2 (i.e. Habc and H3) via a non-conserved linker with variable lengths in different homologs (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the figures.

claim: The NPY motifs bind individually to Sec3 in the two structural copies.
source: These NPY motifs bind individually to Sec3 in the two structural copies (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in the figures.

claim: The tyrosine residues in both NPY motifs (i.e. Y7 and Y13) are docked into a conserved hydrophobic pocket on the concave surface on Sec3.
source: Particularly, the tyrosine residues in both cases (i.e. Y7 and Y13) are docked into a conserved hydrophobic pocket on the concave surface on Sec3 (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in the figures.

claim: The NPY motif adopts a T-shaped conformation, with its broad top part shaped by the asparagine (N) and the proline (P) residues, which is stabilized by a hydrogen bond between the carboxyl group of the asparagine and the amide proton of the proline.
source: Overall, the NPY motif adopts a T-shaped conformation, with its broad top part shaped by the asparagine (N) and the proline (P) residues, which is stabilized by a hydrogen bond between the carboxyl group of the asparagine and the amide proton of the proline (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The tyrosine residue sticks out to form a pin-like structure that fits neatly in the pocket on Sec3.
source: The tyrosine residue sticks out to form a pin-like structure that fits neatly in the pocket on Sec3.
evidence: This is a structural description based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Wild type double NPY motifs of Sso2 (aa1–15) bound Sec3 with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 21.1 µM.
source: Wild type (WT) double NPY motifs of Sso2 (aa1–15) bound Sec3 with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 21.1 µM (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Each NPY motif individually bound Sec3 much more weakly, with binding affinities reduced by three- to fourfold.
source: However, each NPY motif individually bound Sec3 much more weakly, with binding affinities reduced by three- to fourfold (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figures 3B and C.

claim: Mutation of all core residues of the first NPY motif to alanines (M5) slightly reduced the binding affinity (Kd = 34.9 µM).
source: Mutation of all core residues of the first NPY motif to alanines (M5) slightly reduced the binding affinity (Kd = 34.9 µM) (Figure 3D), whereas mutation of the second NPY motif (M6) drastically affected the interaction, with a Kd of 188 µM (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutation of the second NPY motif (M6) drastically affected the interaction, with a Kd of 188 µM.
source: Mutation of all core residues of the first NPY motif to alanines (M5) slightly reduced the binding affinity (Kd = 34.9 µM) (Figure 3D), whereas mutation of the second NPY motif (M6) drastically affected the interaction, with a Kd of 188 µM (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The synthetic polypeptide with both NPY motifs mutated (M7) displayed no detectable interaction with Sec3.
source: The synthetic polypeptide with both NPY motifs mutated (M7) displayed no detectable interaction with Sec3 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: No effect on growth was observed with single, double, or triple mutations in the first NPY domain (sso1Δ sso2M1-M4).
source: No effect was observed with single, double, or triple mutations in the first NPY domain (sso1Δ sso2M1-M4), however changing all four residues to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M5) resulted in reduced growth at 37°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Changing all four residues of the first NPY domain to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M5) resulted in reduced growth at 37°C.
source: No effect was observed with single, double, or triple mutations in the first NPY domain (sso1Δ sso2M1-M4), however changing all four residues to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M5) resulted in reduced growth at 37°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutating all four residues of the second NPY domain to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M6) did not affect growth at any temperature.
source: Mutating all four residues of the second NPY domain to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M6) did not affect growth at any temperature, however changing all residues of both the first and second NPY domain to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M7) resulted in significantly reduced growth at both 25°C and 34°C and severely impaired growth at 37°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Changing all residues of both the first and second NPY domain to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M7) resulted in significantly reduced growth at both 25°C and 34°C and severely impaired growth at 37°C.
source: Mutating all four residues of the second NPY domain to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M6) did not affect growth at any temperature, however changing all residues of both the first and second NPY domain to alanine (sso1Δ sso2M7) resulted in significantly reduced growth at both 25°C and 34°C and severely impaired growth at 37°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The synergistic effects of eliminating the first and second NPY motif of Sso2 suggest that both motifs are functional and at least partially redundant.
source: The synergistic effects of eliminating the first and second NPY motif of Sso2 suggest that both motifs are functional and at least partially redundant.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the growth assay data showing that double mutation has a stronger effect than single mutations.

claim: Several mutations in SSO2 caused inhibition of Bgl2 secretion.
source: The internal or external pools of Bgl2 were detected by western blotting. Several mutations in SSO2 caused inhibition of Bgl2 secretion.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: sso1Δ sso2M1-M6 showed only a modest accumulation of an internal pool of Bgl2.
source: Using western blot analysis to measure the internal and external pools of Bgl2, we found that the secretory efficiency at 37°C generally paralleled growth: sso1Δ sso2M1-M6 showed only a modest accumulation of an internal pool, while sso1Δ sso2M7 accumulated a significantly larger internal pool (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4C and D.

claim: sso1Δ sso2M7 accumulated a significantly larger internal pool of Bgl2.
source: Using western blot analysis to measure the internal and external pools of Bgl2, we found that the secretory efficiency at 37°C generally paralleled growth: sso1Δ sso2M1-M6 showed only a modest accumulation of an internal pool, while sso1Δ sso2M7 accumulated a significantly larger internal pool (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4C and D.

claim: sso1Δ sso2M1-M4 and sso1Δ sso2M6 were not significantly different from the sso1Δ SSO2 control in invertase secretion.
source: Using these conditions we found that sso1Δ sso2M1-M4 and sso1Δ sso2M6 were not significantly different from the sso1Δ SSO2 control, while sso1Δ sso2M5 showed a minor defect in invertase secretion and sso1Δ sso2M7 showed a more substantial defect (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by invertase secretion assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: sso1Δ sso2M5 showed a minor defect in invertase secretion.
source: Using these conditions we found that sso1Δ sso2M1-M4 and sso1Δ sso2M6 were not significantly different from the sso1Δ SSO2 control, while sso1Δ sso2M5 showed a minor defect in invertase secretion and sso1Δ sso2M7 showed a more substantial defect (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by invertase secretion assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: sso1Δ sso2M7 showed a more substantial defect in invertase secretion.
source: Using these conditions we found that sso1Δ sso2M1-M4 and sso1Δ sso2M6 were not significantly different from the sso1Δ SSO2 control, while sso1Δ sso2M5 showed a minor defect in invertase secretion and sso1Δ sso2M7 showed a more substantial defect (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by invertase secretion assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Loss of function of exocytic SNAREs, including Sso1 and Sso2, leads to the accumulation of secretory vesicles.
source: Loss of function of exocytic SNAREs, including Sso1 and Sso2, leads to the accumulation of secretory vesicles (Aalto et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Secretory vesicles are normally delivered to sites of polarized cell surface growth, such as the tip of the bud, early in the cell cycle, and the neck separating the mother cell and bud, late in the cell cycle.
source: Secretory vesicles are normally delivered to sites of polarized cell surface growth, such as the tip of the bud, early in the cell cycle, and the neck separating the mother cell and bud, late in the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast cell biology.

claim: The sso1Δ SSO2 control and the sso1Δ sso2M6 mutant had relatively few vesicles per cell section.
source: Thin section electron microscopy revealed an accumulation of vesicles in the mutants that mirrored their growth: the sso1Δ SSO2 control and the sso1Δ sso2M6 mutant had relatively few vesicles per cell section, while sso1Δ sso2M5 and sso1Δ sso2M7 had many more (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: sso1Δ sso2M5 and sso1Δ sso2M7 had many more vesicles per cell section than the control.
source: Thin section electron microscopy revealed an accumulation of vesicles in the mutants that mirrored their growth: the sso1Δ SSO2 control and the sso1Δ sso2M6 mutant had relatively few vesicles per cell section, while sso1Δ sso2M5 and sso1Δ sso2M7 had many more (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The vesicles were similar in size in the different strains.
source: The vesicles were similar in size in the different strains (Figure 5F) and were found preferentially within the buds of small budded cells (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by vesicle size measurements shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The vesicles were found preferentially within the buds of small budded cells.
source: The vesicles were similar in size in the different strains (Figure 5F) and were found preferentially within the buds of small budded cells (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: The Snc1 v-SNARE has been shown to rapidly cycle from secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane, and then into endocytic vesicles from which it is recycled through the Golgi into a new round of secretory vesicles.
source: The Snc1 v-SNARE has been shown to rapidly cycle from secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane, and then into endocytic vesicles from which it is recycled through the Golgi into a new round of secretory vesicles (Lewis et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Under normal growth conditions, Snc1 is predominantly found on the plasma membrane, with only a minor pool in internal structures.
source: Under normal growth conditions, Snc1 is predominantly found on the plasma membrane, with only a minor pool in internal structures.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Snc1 localization.

claim: Impeding any step in the Snc1 cycle leads to a shift in the steady-state distribution of GFP-Snc1.
source: Impeding any step in the cycle leads to a shift in the steady-state distribution of GFP-Snc1.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the cycling behavior of Snc1.

claim: In the sso1Δ SSO2 control and the sso1Δ sso2M6 mutant, GFP-Snc1 was mostly on the plasma membrane with a small number of internal, patch-like structures apparent.
source: In the sso1Δ SSO2 control and the sso1Δ sso2M6 mutant, GFP-Snc1 was mostly on the plasma membrane with a small number of internal, patch-like structures apparent (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The sso1Δ sso2M5 and sso1Δ sso2M7 mutants showed a much greater fraction of cells with internal patches of GFP-Snc1, presumably representing concentrations of secretory vesicles, and a greatly reduced localization to the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, the sso1Δ sso2M5 and sso1Δ sso2M7 mutants showed a much greater fraction of cells with internal patches of GFP-Snc1, presumably representing concentrations of secretory vesicles, and a greatly reduced localization to the plasma membrane (Figure 6B, D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Secretory vesicles are delivered to sites of cell surface growth by the type V myosin, Myo2, moving along polarized actin cables.
source: Secretory vesicles are delivered to sites of cell surface growth by the type V myosin, Myo2, moving along polarized actin cables (Pruyne et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of actin or Myo2 function leads to the rapid depolarization of a vesicle marker, such as the Rab GTPase Sec4.
source: Loss of actin or Myo2 function leads to the rapid depolarization of a vesicle marker, such as the Rab GTPase Sec4 (Salminen and Novick, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Sec3 remains associated with the tips of small buds and the necks of large buds even after actin polymerization has been blocked by addition of Latrunculin A (LatA).
source: Sec3, in contrast, remains associated with the tips of small buds and the necks of large buds even after actin polymerization has been blocked by addition of Latrunculin A (LatA) (Finger et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The polarized localization of GFP-Sec4 was lost after treatment with LatA.
source: The polarized localization of GFP-Sec4 was lost after treatment with LatA (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The localization of Sec3−3×GFP was largely resistant to LatA treatment in the control and sso1Δ sso2M5 mutant cells.
source: While the localization of Sec3−3×GFP was largely resistant to LatA treatment in the control and sso1Δ sso2M5 mutant cells, the polarization of Sec3−3×GFP in sso1Δ sso2M7 was only slightly reduced by LatA treatment (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The polarization of Sec3−3×GFP in sso1Δ sso2M7 was only slightly reduced by LatA treatment.
source: While the localization of Sec3−3×GFP was largely resistant to LatA treatment in the control and sso1Δ sso2M5 mutant cells, the polarization of Sec3−3×GFP in sso1Δ sso2M7 was only slightly reduced by LatA treatment (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The NPY motifs of Sso2 do not play a major role in the recruitment of Sec3 to sites of polarized growth.
source: These results demonstrate that the NPY motifs of Sso2 do not play a major role in the recruitment of Sec3 to sites of polarized growth.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the LatA treatment data showing that Sec3 localization is maintained even in the M7 mutant.

claim: The actin-independent localization of Sec3 involves its interaction with the Rho1 and Cdc42 GTPases.
source: Notably, prior studies have shown that the actin-independent localization of Sec3 involves its interaction with the Rho1 and Cdc42 GTPases (Guo et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The M7 mutant of Sso2 (aa1–270) completely abolished its interaction with the Sec3 PH domain.
source: Our ITC data reveal that the M7 mutant of Sso2 (aa1–270) completely abolished its interaction with the Sec3 PH domain (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Wild type Sso2 (aa1–270) bound Sec3 robustly, with Kd ~ 2.7 µM.
source: Our results show that WT Sso2 bound Sec3 robustly, with Kd ~ 2.7 µM (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The NPY motifs play an essential role in stabilizing the interaction between Sso2 and Sec3.
source: All these demonstrate that the NPY motifs play an essential role in stabilizing the interaction between Sso2 and Sec3.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ITC, EMSA, SEC, and co-IP data showing that the M7 mutant abolishes the interaction.

claim: The dual interaction interfaces between Sso2 and Sec3 are reminiscent of what has been seen in the structures of syntaxin-1 and Tlg2 in complex with their partner SM proteins Munc18 and Vps45, respectively.
source: The dual interaction interfaces between Sso2 and Sec3 are reminiscent of what has been seen in the structures of syntaxin-1 and Tlg2 in complex with their partner SM proteins Munc18 and Vps45, respectively (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis based on structural similarities with previously published structures.

claim: In the Munc18/syntaxin-1 and Vps45/Tlg2 complex structures, a short peptide at the N-terminus of Munc-18 and Vps45, which was named 'N-peptide', forms a short helix and binds distally to the backside of the first domain of Munc18 or Vps45, opposite to their interaction sites with the helical bundles of the SNARE proteins.
source: In the latter two complex structures, a short peptide at the N-terminus of Munc-18 and Vps45, which was named 'N-peptide', forms a short helix and binds distally to the backside of the first domain of Munc18 or Vps45, opposite to their interaction sites with the helical bundles of the SNARE proteins (Eisemann et al., 2020; Burkhardt et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The binding site for the NPY motifs of Sso2 is on the same side of the Sec3 PH domain as the direct contact with the C-terminal part of H3 of Sso2.
source: In contrast, the binding site for the NPY motifs of Sso2 is on the same side of the Sec3 PH domain as the aforementioned direct contact with the C-terminal part of H3 of Sso2 (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure data.

claim: The Sec3 PH domain is a single globular domain and much smaller than Munc18 and Vps45, both of which contain three domains that are folded into a horseshoe-like conformation.
source: Furthermore, the Sec3 PH domain is a single globular domain and much smaller than Munc18 and Vps45, both of which contain three domains that are folded into a horseshoe-like conformation.
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis based on known structures.

claim: The helical bundle of syntaxin-1 and Tlg2 is clamped between the two tips of the 'horseshoe' in their complexes with SM proteins.
source: The helical bundle of syntaxin-1 and Tlg2 is clamped between the two tips of the 'horseshoe'.
evidence: This is a structural description based on previously published structures.

claim: In the Munc18/syntaxin-1 and Vps45/Tlg2 complex structures, the C-terminal extensions of the SNARE motifs (i.e. H3) form a short helix and insert into a hydrophobic pocket deeply inside the 'horseshoe'.
source: Additionally, in those two complex structures, the C-terminal extensions of the SNARE motifs (i.e. H3) form a short helix and insert into a hydrophobic pocket deeply inside the 'horseshoe' (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is a structural description based on previously published structures.

claim: The interaction interface between Sec3 and Sso2 is very small, and thus their interaction is presumably much weaker than that in the Munc18/syntaxin-1 and Vps45/Tlg2 complexes.
source: In contrast, the interaction interface between Sec3 and Sso2 is very small, and thus their interaction is presumably much weaker than that in the Munc18/syntaxin-1 and Vps45/Tlg2 complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural comparison.

claim: Double mutation of both NPY motifs substantially impaired protein secretion as well as recycling of cell surface proteins.
source: Consistently, our in vivo data demonstrate that simultaneous mutation of both NPY motifs substantially impaired protein secretion as well as recycling of cell surface proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Bgl2, invertase, and GFP-Snc1 data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NPY motifs play an important role in stabilizing the interaction of Sso2 with Sec3 by providing an additional binding site, which ensures effective recruitment of Sso2 to vesicle-docking sites on the plasma membrane.
source: We therefore think that the NPY motifs play an important role in stabilizing the interaction of Sso2 with Sec3 by providing an additional binding site, which ensures effective recruitment of Sso2 to vesicle-docking sites on the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the structural and functional data presented in the study.

claim: Another possible role for the NPY motifs might be to serve as a stopper to hold the destabilized SNARE motif in place to prevent a premature release of H3 before the right time comes for it to form a binary complex with the other t-SNARE protein Sec9.
source: Given that binding of Sec3 destabilizes the linker connecting H3 to Hc and prepares H3 for its subsequent interaction with Sec9, we think that another possible role for the NPY motifs, which are packed tightly against the C-terminal tip of the SNARE motif H3 (Figure 8A and B), might be to serve as a stopper to hold the destabilized SNARE motif in place to prevent a premature release of H3 before the right time comes for it to form a binary complex with the other t-SNARE protein Sec9.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the structural observation that the NPY motifs contact the C-terminal tip of H3.

claim: The N-peptide motif is ubiquitously present in all syntaxins that interact with SM proteins.
source: Notably, the N-peptide motif is ubiquitously present in all syntaxins that interact with SM proteins (Latham et al., 2006; McEwen and Kaplan, 2008; Johnson et al., 2009; Khvotchev et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The N-peptide motif serves as an initiator to recruit SM proteins to their SNARE partners to facilitate their subsequent assembly.
source: It serves as an initiator to recruit SM proteins to their SNARE partners to facilitate their subsequent assembly (Rathore et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The NPY motifs may function like fishing hooks to search for Sec3 around the membrane-anchored Sso2.
source: Given that the NPY motifs are connected to the rest of Sso2 via a long variable linker, we hypothesize that they may similarly function like fishing hooks to search for Sec3 around the membrane-anchored Sso2 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the structural features of the NPY motifs and their linker.

claim: Once the NPY motifs find and bind to Sec3, Sso2 would be locally restrained, which would promote the binding of Sec3 to the helical bundle of Sso2.
source: Once the 'hooks' find and bind to Sec3, Sso2 would be locally restrained, which would promote the binding of Sec3 to the helical bundle of Sso2.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the dual-site binding model.

claim: Binding of Sec3 to the helical bundle would lead to the destabilization of the linker between Hc and H3 of Sso2 and thus promote the assembly of the binary complex between Sso2 and Sec9 to facilitate the final formation of the full SNARE complex with the v-SNARE Snc1/2.
source: This would in turn lead to the destabilization of the linker between Hc and H3 of Sso2 and thus promote the assembly of the binary complex between Sso2 and Sec9 to facilitate the final formation of the full SNARE complex with the v-SNARE Snc1/2, which eventually drives the fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model integrating the current findings with previous work on Sec3-mediated SNARE assembly.

claim: The full SNARE complex assembly eventually drives the fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane.
source: This would in turn lead to the destabilization of the linker between Hc and H3 of Sso2 and thus promote the assembly of the binary complex between Sso2 and Sec9 to facilitate the final formation of the full SNARE complex with the v-SNARE Snc1/2, which eventually drives the fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about SNARE-mediated membrane fusion.

claim: The crystal structure contains residues 4–8 of Sso2 with clear densities in the 2Fo–Fc map in one complex.
source: In one complex structure, residues 4–8 of Sso2 show clear densities in the 2Fo–Fc map (Figure 2C) in the other structure we could unambiguously trace sidechains of residues 10–14, but for residues 6–9 we could build only the backbone atoms (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a description of the electron density quality in the crystal structure.

claim: Despite variations in the flanking residues of the NPY motifs, the NPY cores adopt essentially the same conformation and share similar contacts with ordered solvent molecules and neighboring residues from Sec3.
source: Despite variations in the flanking residues of these NPY motifs, the NPY cores adopt essentially the same conformation and share similar contacts with ordered solvent molecules and neighboring residues from Sec3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure data.

claim: The 'fuzzy' part upstream of the bound NPY motif is in close contact with the C-terminal tip of the SNARE motif (i.e. H3) of Sso2.
source: We found that this 'fuzzy' part upstream of the bound NPY motif is in close contact with the C-terminal tip of the SNARE motif (i.e. H3) of Sso2 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure data.

claim: Size exclusion chromatography shows that Sec3 could form complex with only WT but not the M7 mutant of Sso2.
source: Consistently, our further test using SEC also shows that Sec3 could form complex with only WT but not the M7 mutant of Sso2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In contrast to the clear signal of WT Sso2 pulled down by Sec3−3×Flag, the pull-down band for the M7 mutant was much weaker and near the level of the negative control in which the Sec3−3×Flag was absent.
source: Our results show that, in contrast to the clear signal of WT Sso2 pulled down by Sec3−3×Flag, the pull-down band for the M7 mutant was much weaker and near the level of the negative control in which the Sec3−3×Flag was absent (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.
